Transcript:
00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we're excited to run through the edge cases demo today, we've got daniel on the call to walk through the runtime and the benchmark, and then we'll leave time for Q&A, sound good?
00:09 Priya Rao: yep sounds good, thanks Maya. we've got about an hour. we want to see how you handle long transcripts and what happens when we push high tps with streaming clients.
00:18 Daniel Ortiz: great, quick agenda. first a quick architecture recap, then live demo: long context with 150k-ish tokens prefix (note: synthetic but representative), then a high-TPS write with streaming responses demonstrating backpressure, then timeouts and fallbacks, and finally ops and security notes.
00:35 Evan Li: quick qual question — what do you consider long-context? is it >64k or more? our primary use-case is multi-document summarization where context can be 80-120k tokens.
00:43 Daniel Ortiz: yeah, for us long-context means anything beyond typical 32k sequences; we support variants up to 200k in Dedicated/Private deployments with chunked KV cache and off-VM storage for embeddings. the demo will show a ~100k token prefix.
00:58 Samir Patel: also side note — we need to understand the performance at scale. we're looking at 500-1000 TPS for short requests across many users, and then occasional bursts to 5k TPS for thumbnailing-type calls.
01:10 Maya Chen: totally. we'll show throughput profiles and the Console's Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization later.
01:22 Daniel Ortiz: ok jumping in — architecture slide — (audio: slight screen-share shuffle) the runtime combines continuous batching and a KV cache; for long contexts we maintain per-session KV shards so we can avoid re-computing prefixes each request — there can be some networked kv hits if the cache is off-host.
01:40 Evan Li: when you say off-host, is it S3-based or a low-latency store? latency matters a lot.
01:46 Daniel Ortiz: good question — by default in Hosted it's a high-throughput in-memory tier; Dedicated/Private can be configured to use local NVMe-backed cache or a regionally colocated low-latency store. the overhead for a remote KV miss is typically 10-40ms extra per segment depending on region.
02:05 Priya Rao: ok, show us the demo.
02:10 Daniel Ortiz: demo: loading prefix — note there's a bit of transcription noise: demo scripts say 'loadin prefix' heh. loading a 100k token context now, you'll see initial load time ~3.2s to warm the kv shards, subsequent queries that share prefix are low ms.
02:28 Evan Li: do you compress the KV? because 100k tokens is heavy.
02:33 Daniel Ortiz: we use quantized KV blobs and delta-compressed embeddings; also we chunk keys so we only fetch the relevant window for generation.
02:40 Maya Chen: timeline note — after we warm the cache, per-request latency for a typical generate is 30-120ms p50/p95 depending on sequence length. p99 can be higher for first-time cold sessions.
02:52 Samir Patel: can you surface those p99 spikes in Console alerts? we need alerting on latency regressions.
02:58 Daniel Ortiz: yep Console has p50/p95/p99 charts and you can create regression alerts tied to prompt-sets. we'll show the dashboard.
03:07 Daniel Ortiz: ok switching to high-TPS streaming scenario — we're going to push synthetic traffic at 3k TPS for short requests with streaming enabled. note: streaming introduces backpressure dynamics because the client reads partial frames.
03:24 (sound: typing)
03:30 Daniel Ortiz: starting load — streaming clients here maintain a small window on in-flight tokens and if the server faces queue growth we shed by delaying next batch and prioritizing low-latency routes. you can configure routing policies: latency-first, cost-first, or regional.
03:46 Evan Li: what does backpressure look like on the wire? does the server pause generating or does it buffer?
03:52 Daniel Ortiz: we stream in incremental frames; when the client socket is slow the runtime will buffer up to a configurable threshold (default 4MB) then apply backpressure by slowing generation for that connection and eventually returning a 429-like spike for overloaded routes if the queue exceeds capacity. clients see chunk delays rather than sudden drops.
04:12 Priya Rao: hmm 429-like, do you have client-side retry recommendations? e.g. linear vs exponential backoff? we can't afford to retry naively and overwhelm the system.
04:22 Daniel Ortiz: recommended is jittered exponential with a max total retry window; Combine with client-side circuit breaker based on observed chunk delays. Console's Optimize suggests batching parameters that reduce contention.
04:32 Maya Chen: also note we have automatic fallback policies — if Hosted capacity is constrained we can route to a cheaper variant or to Dedicated if you have reserved pools; the Console shows cost/latency tradeoffs.
04:45 Samir Patel: in private deploys do you support the same streaming protocol or is it different?
04:49 Daniel Ortiz: same protocol, it's our API; the implementation differs only in the runtime placement. Private customers control the network and can drop the remote kv into local NVMe for better tail latency.
05:00 Evan Li: we'd like to see a pathological case — many concurrent long-context sessions where prefix can't be fully cached. what happens when requests saturate memory?
05:10 Daniel Ortiz: good one — the runtime enforces per-session cache quotas and will evict least-recent shards; for active sessions we keep hot windows; if memory saturates we throttle new session creation and surface backpressure to clients. you can configure eviction policy and warm-start rules in Dedicated.
05:26 Priya Rao: okay please demo the timeout/fallback behavior.
05:30 Daniel Ortiz: demo: I'll artificially slow one of the streaming clients to trigger backpressure, you'll see chunk latencies climb, after threshold the runtime responds with a partial result and a 'streaming timeout' marker, and our SDK will surface a specific error code so apps can decide to retry or serve degraded content.
05:50 Evan Li: does partial result mean truncated output? our UX needs to indicate incomplete answers.
:05:56 Daniel Ortiz: yes truncated; we also emit a structured metadata frame indicating 'incomplete=true' and include tokens completed and a recommended retry strategy.
06:10 Priya Rao: is that metadata standardized across SDKs?
06:14 Maya Chen: yes, it's in our SDK spec; we'll share the link. Daniel will drop the spec in the benchmark repo.
06:20 (brief cross-talk)
06:30 Daniel Ortiz: moving to ops and security — we support SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, SOC2 cert, and customer-managed KMS for Private deployments. logs include token-level latency and routing decisions for debugging.
06:45 Samir Patel: can audit logs be forwarded to our SIEM? we need long retention.
06:50 Daniel Ortiz: yes, you can ship logs to your S3 or SIEM; Dedicated has configurable retention and Private you control retention entirely.
06:58 Priya Rao: pricing — can you give a ballpark for a 6-month pilot with 500-1000 TPS steady and a burst profile?
07:06 Maya Chen: ballpark depends on caching and quantization; we typically propose a Dedicated pilot with reserved pool + host overage. I'll send a tailored SOW but ballpark monthly committed spend in the mid 6 figures for that scale.
07:18 Evan Li: acceptable, we expected that, need the exact model of cost vs p95 latency.
07:23 Daniel Ortiz: Console's Optimize can produce cost/latency curves; we'll export examples in the benchmark sheet.
07:30 Priya Rao: any known gotchas? we've had issues with previous vendors where streaming timeouts caused double-billing or duplicate outputs.
07:38 Daniel Ortiz: good callout. we include idempotency keys and per-request billing events at completion; partials don't bill full; dedupe guidance is in the SDK docs.
07:50 Samir Patel: on the private side, what's the upgrade path if we need more capacity quickly?
07:55 Maya Chen: Dedicated offers burst capacity pools and we can deploy extra nodes; Private can be scaled by your infra team but we can provide automation playbooks.
08:05 Evan Li: for the benchmark run, we'd like to replicate our topology: 1) 80-120k token prefix on 200 concurrent sessions 2) 1k TPS short streaming requests 3) Burst to 5k TPS for 30s — can you run these?
08:20 Daniel Ortiz: yes we can run all three; we'll need your sample prompts and expected latencies. we'll also instrument client-side to capture chunk delays.
08:28 Priya Rao: security docs?
08:30 Maya Chen: will attach SOC2 pack, architecture whitepaper, and KMS integration guide.
08:35 Evan Li: ok if we sign a pilot can we get a week of dedicated benchmarking with support from an SE?
08:40 Maya Chen: yes, SE support included for pilots. we'll propose a 2-week engagement: week one test setup, week two ramp and collection.
08:48 (brief pause)
08:52 Priya Rao: one last question — how do you handle model rollouts? we need to pin versions and do canarying.
08:57 Daniel Ortiz: rollouts are through Console: you can pin model versions, do canary percentages per route, and automatic rollback on quality regressions tied to eval prompt sets.
09:08 Samir Patel: great.
09:10 Maya Chen: ok recap — next steps: I'll send pricing & SOW, Dan will share benchmark sheet and harness repo, Evan to provide sample prompts, we'll schedule a 2-hour run next wk.
09:21 Priya Rao: perfect, thanks everyone.
09:24 Maya Chen: thanks, talk soon.
